newsitem.title: USA: Enamelon off amid new report of short-selling.
newsitem.headline: Enamelon off amid new report of short-selling.

text.p: Shares of Enamelon Inc dropped 10 percent after a media report said a money manager is shorting the stock because he believes it is overvalued.

An April 21 Business Week report said the unnamed money manager doubts Enamelon's earnings and sales will be able to justify its current stock price. The money manager said Enamelon would have to earn a $1 a share on sales of $150 million to explain its high-flying stock value, Business Week reported.

Enamelon, which has begun test marketing a new toothpaste designed to prevent cavities, dropped 1-3/4 to 20-3/4 on Friday. Enamelon's stock had risen as high at 24-1/4 in recent weeks after the company presented its clinical research data at a dental confernce.

Enamelon's chairman Steven Fox said the Business Week report is off-base. Fox said the new toothpaste is even more significant to the oral care industry than Procter & Gamble Co's Crest with fluoride, introduced in the 1950s.

Enamelon's toothpaste strengthens tooth enamel from the inside out by adding calcium, phosphate and fluoide ions to teeth during brushing. The ions are designed to enter the teeth and create a stronger molecular structure.
Fox said he expects Enamelon to seize a sizable portion of the $5 to $10 billion worldwide oral care market.

"When people begin learning about the product, hearing about it from their dentists and seeing the commercials, don't you think that at least 10 percent of the market will want to buy it? That's $500 million in sales, at least. The potential is just unknown," Fox said.

Enamelon has 18 patents and pending patents covering toothpaste, mouthwash, gum, candy and other food products. The company is currently test marketing the toothpaste in two cities and expects to launch the product nationally in the first quarter of 1998.
Gum, mouthwash and other products are still in development.
"If we focus on doing our job and doing it affectively, I'm sure the stock price will follow," said Stephen Fox.
Enamelon's toothpaste, also called Enamelon, will face a tough battle against leading products such as Crest and Colgate-Palmolive Co's Colgate, analysts said.
The toothpaste giants have stronger markering, advertising and distribution muscle than Yonkers, N.Y.-based Enamelon, which launched its initial public offering in October.
Crest and Colgate together hold about 47 percent of the toothpaste market, but their dominance has slipped slightly since new toothpastes have attracted customers, analysts said.
Enamelon could benefit from consumers' willingness to try different toothpaste products, analysts said.
Eventually, Enamelon may become an acquistion target since its patents would be valuable assets for the major toothpaste makers, analysts said.
